title: German MCP Report 2026: How agent-ready are 21 German B2B SaaS APIs?
intro:
AI agents (Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot & Co.) can only operate software on their own if the API is built for it: an MCP endpoint (Model Context Protocol), clean OAuth-standard authentication, machine-readable documentation. We put the APIs of 21 German B2B SaaS providers from the office and accounting software, ERP, HR, e-commerce, real estate, and communications sectors through a public surface assessment, using the same automated test our free MCP live test runs for every API.

Only the public surface was tested (no credentials, no write access): MCP handshake, OAuth discovery per RFC 9728/8414, OpenAPI availability, agent crawler policy in robots.txt, server card candidates. Supplemented by manual research into official announcements and community projects.
keyFindings: **3 of 21 companies offer an official MCP server: awork, seven.io, and clockodo.** All endpoints pass our live test with clean OAuth discovery (RFC 9728). The rest of the industry is absent from a technology the market already treats as a standard.
**No company reaches half of the possible 100 points.** Best in class: awork at 53/100, making it the German benchmark. The field's median sits at 8 of 100 points.

**14 of 21 provide no machine-readable API description.** Without an OpenAPI spec, every agent integration remains a hand-built GitHub repository, failure modes included. Exactly such unofficial wrappers already exist for at least 8 of the tested products.

**The demand exists without the supply:** Zammad customers ask for MCP in the official forum (561 views), the vendor's answer is “not really planned”, while a community server collects 41 stars. Personio, Propstack, and Xentral now ship llms.txt for AI systems but offer no agent access to the product.

**Authentication is the blind spot:** 9 of the 21 APIs work with static keys and no OAuth flow. Delegated, restricted agent access (“this agent may only read invoices”) is technically impossible as a result.
methodology:
Tested per company: (1) MCP endpoint at the documented address; for vendors without a documented endpoint, derived hosts (mcp./api./docs./developers./developer. of the vendor domain) are additionally checked with a handshake scan: initialize/tools/list, Streamable HTTP, legacy SSE fallback, protocol version incl. server/discover per specification 2026-07-28; (2) authentication signals: 401/403 behavior, WWW-Authenticate with resource_metadata, OAuth Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728), Authorization Server Metadata (RFC 8414); (3) MCP Server Card (working group draft: /.well-known/mcp.json among others); (4) documentation surface: OpenAPI/Swagger at standard paths, at addresses verified during research and, if no spec is found there, on derived hosts (docs./api./developers./developer. of the vendor domain), robots.txt policies for 13 known AI crawlers (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot among others), llms.txt (rated as cosmetic, since a Google study from 6/2026 found no effect), security.txt.

Scoring: 40 points for a real MCP offering (handshake 15, listable tools 10, current specification level 5, server card 10), 25 points for authentication and safety signals, 20 points for machine-readable documentation, 15 points for tool description quality. The point distribution is deliberately designed so that a company without an MCP offering cannot mathematically reach the top grade. A dozen blog articles do not replace an endpoint.

Limitations: The assessment is a snapshot of the public surface (September 19–20, 2026; corrected run on September 22, 2026, after the detection of specs at standard paths was repaired: sevdesk turns out to have a previously overlooked OpenAPI spec at api.sevdesk.de/openapi.yaml; a second full run with extended host detection confirmed all remaining values) and does not replace a security audit. What this test cannot see (live runs of real agents, tool permissions in detail, tenant separation, GDPR data flows) is the subject of our paid audit.
